data.content_ref: inline:The target proposes 'difficulty-correlated cognitive friction' (operationalized as a 'time-spike' on harder items) as the sole evidence that distinguishes genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance. But this fails the problem as stated: it does not identify what evidence within a single evaluation would distinguish genuine reliability from compliance that happens to track the right answer. A panel can spend more time on hard items due to confusion, inefficiency, or difficulty interpreting the checklist — producing the exact predicted time-spike — while not actually verifying more accurately. Conversely, genuine reliability gains can arise from a well-calibrated checklist that makes verification faster and more uniform (less friction), not slower. The proposed evidence is neither necessary nor sufficient: it confuses effort with correctness. The problem asks for evidence that separates genuine reliability from compliance tracking the right answer; the target offers a proxy that can be satisfied by either side and violated by the other. No single-evaluation result per the target's own criterion would reliably distinguish the two.
